title: Westpac, ANZ chiefs tell MPs that mortgage pain is just starting
full_text:
Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller has warned that the number of customers falling three months behind on mortgage repayments could rise by more than a third over the next year as five interest rate rises since February and higher inflation put intense pressure on family budgets.
Miller made the comments as he appeared before a parliamentary inquiry, one day after Commonwealth Bank reported its 90-day arrears, a closely watched metric of mortgages at risk, had hit a 14-year-high of 0.80 per cent.
“We know that many are doing it tough,” Miller said, adding he expected arrears to rise as they had in 2022 and 2023, the last time that the Reserve Bank of Australia sharply increased rates to tame inflation.
Such an increase would lift Westpac’s mortgages in arrear from 0.67 per cent at the end of September to between 0.79 per cent and 0.91 per cent over the next 12 months – a 36 per cent increase at the top end.
The RBA has pushed rates up five times since February, most recently earlier this month, to 4.85 per cent, its highest level in 18 years.
Senior figures at the country’s major banks are appearing before a parliamentary inquiry this week, with Miller following ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos. National Australia Bank chief executive Andrew Irvine and CBA’s Matt Comyn are scheduled to appear at the inquiry on Friday.
Matos had told the committee that higher arrears would appear across every major bank. In its full-year results this week, ANZ said 0.95 per cent of borrowers were three months or more behind on home loan payments.
“It is on the rise because cost of living is on the rise,” Matos said. “We should expect those numbers to continue to deteriorate. I don’t expect them to go to a historically bad place, but they will get worse before they get better.”
The number of ANZ borrowers in negative equity – owing the bank more than their house is now worth – is now at 2.3 per cent having risen steadily from 1.7 per cent 12 months ago as house prices fall. Hardship cases had increased by 10 per cent over the last six months but at five in 1000, stress remains low, and the banking system well-capitalised, Matos added.
ANZ CEO Nuno Matos said the level of mortgage arrears was set to increase. Alex Ellinghausen
Regulators are also watching arrears. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority said on Thursday that risks to broader financial system’s stability would increase if a sharper fall in housing prices coincided with a substantial rise in unemployment or tighter credit conditions.
“For affected households, this could mean greater difficulty keeping up with repayments, a need to cut spending or, in some cases, having to sell their property,” the regulator said in an annual update on risks.
“Aggregate household debt is around 180 per cent of disposable income, which is high by historical and international standards. Highly indebted households and those with limited buffers have less capacity to absorb income losses or higher living costs,” the regulator added.
ANZ, Westpac and NAB all observed rising stress across their mortgage books when delivering their full-year results earlier this month. NAB increased its provisioning buffers as it expected more small business owners to struggle including, by extension, with their home loans.
The tough economic environment was also pressuring small business further as consumer and business confidence runs low, Matos said.
“It is very clear that the credit conditions for companies are not improving. In our central scenario, this won’t result in a crisis – but it’s certainly a scenario where it’s not inviting growth at this point in time,” he added.
Economists surveyed by The Australian Financial Review earlier this month broadly expect the RBA not to increase rates again, adding the central bank would face an uncomfortable call given the pressure on families.
Those pressures have created a significant headwind for the government, and for Treasurer Jim Chalmers, with senior colleagues including Environment Minister Murray Watt publicly calling for Labor MPs to stop undermining him even as they worried about higher inflation.
On Thursday, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek told News24 that there were “difficult economic circumstances globally”.
“He’s steadied the ship, and I’d also say, every single time we have a treasurer that is bold, that does difficult things that the nation needs, there’s a pile on,” she said.
“It’s tough, when you are in the main job, when you’re the one who’s responsible for finding the savings, when you’re the one delivering the big changes, to set the country up better for the future, you cop it, and that’s ... just part of the job of being a reforming treasurer.”
While the Coalition has accused the government of presiding over a significant housing downturn, with values falling and applications for new mortgages recording their worst quarter in the three months to September 30, Labor has argued its tax changes have increased the proportion of properties being sold to first home buyers over investors.
Asked about affordability, Miller agreed with Liberal MP Simon Kennedy that the benefit of falling house prices has been offset by higher borrowing costs after the five rate rises this year, adding that a one percentage point increase in rates typically reduces borrowing capacity by 10 per cent.
